utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Thursday, 19th of June. Good afternoon, Witness. Good afternoon to the accused and Defence counsel and the OTP representatives, as well as all the people helping us. A brief reminder, housekeeping matter, the second break will only be 15 minutes long so that we can finish today at 25 past 6.00, so it will be 15 minutes, not 20. Without further ado, Ms. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Good afternoon. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the other microphones be switched off, please. There is a lot of background noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We looked at a document yesterday, the last one that we looked at was 2D 00228. On the 28th of January, 1993, Mr. Arif Pasalic gave an order to prevent any supply of weapons to the HVO in that document. Could we now please look a the next document, it's 2D 00229, this is already an exhibit which means it's been used in the courtroom before. Can you please focus on paragraph 2. This is another document from the 4th Corps command. Mr. Arif Pasalic signed the document roughly a month before the ban in the other border, or rather, after the transport of weapons to the HVO. Paragraph 2 reads: "On the day of 27th February, 1993, the BiH army 4th Corps main coordinator for logistical security on relation of the 4th Corps of the BH army and the SDA headquarters in Zagreb, Hasan Cengic submitted the documents and no longer wishes to coordinate because of parallel distribution of money by the Supreme Command headquarters. Mr. Safet Orucevic successfully performed our main tasks regarding the entrance of goods with the HVO until now." Mr. Akmadzic, there is a reference here to something that you confirmed in chief. You said there was a logistics centre in Croatia being used for the purposes of sending supplies to the BH army, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that, there was several such centres, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In this document Mr. Pasalic says that Mr. Safet Orucevic was successful up until the month of February negotiating the transit of goods for the benefit of the HVO. In the other document we saw him banning any transports of weapons, mines, explosives, manpower for the purposes of the HVO. Do we see a dual standard at work here on the one hand sending weapons to the HVO through HVO-controlled territory and then on the other hand we see that very same commander issuing another order banning any supplies or weapons from passing through the territory under their control for the purposes of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. However, I think there are several persons appearing here and they were not perfectly in agreement among themselves. If you look at this letter I think what it shows is that Mr. Cengic and Mr. Orucevic were not towing the same line as it were. Another thing that this shows is that up until this point the cooperation with the HVO about weapons and other equipment and bringing those in had been very successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, does this tally with what you know about developments at the time quite aside from the document?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this tallies with what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Talking about the weapons supplies I would like to show you another document, the next document in my binder, this is 1D 2458. This is a letter by the Ministry of Energy mining and industry of the BH government dated the 14th of February, 1993. The letter is signed by Minister Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic. The document is addressed to Mr. Arif Pasalic, the commander of the 4th Corps. Have you ever seen this document, because I realize that it was part of the Prlic Defence proofing with you?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. I'm not sure if I had a chance to read it, but it looks familiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In this document Mr. Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic is informing Mr. Pasalic about the circumstances in Mostar. He is telling him about his views or perhaps the government's views on strengthening state authority. That's what the introduction says. Let me ask you something about a portion on page 1 in the English, it's page 2 in the Croatian. I think you have a fairly good Croatian copy on the screen, I'm not sure if you can see it clearly. It's where it says: "Supply of oil products." As prime minister did you know about this communication at the time? It is obvious that it was between this ministry and the 4th Corps command alone, excluding the HVO, they were not part of the process.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time we were receiving oil, it came in as aid shipped to us by a number of different countries. This is about oil derived -- this is about crude oil. We obtained oil-derived products from Croatia among other countries. Mr. Mahmut Cehajic was the energy minister. He had certain powers authorising him to use oil and other types of energy that were available. We did in principle have an agreement about the equal distribution of oil between the HVO and the BH army as well as other citizens of the BH, perhaps Mostar and other such places, and it was also agreed that certain shipments would make it to Sarajevo. Sarajevo was facing huge problems, but the shipments still made it. Nevertheless, if I look at this authorisation, I don't think it entirely denies this right. It is just that the HVO's right to use part of this oil is not specified. Be that as it may, if you look at this letter you can see that Mr. Mahmut Cehajic issued certain orders, disregarding for the moment the political aspect which anyway wasn't something that he was supposed to keep in mind. It's about making sure that the oil got to those places that he specified in good time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, let me try to underline something that I found to be of particular importance during your examination. This document seems to show unequivocally that oil derivatives -- the document claims that there was sufficient quantities of those to meet the basic needs of the population as well as the state bodies. The oil derivatives belonging to the republic, Bosnia and Herzegovina, were reaching the port of Ploca and were being stored in the Energopetrol warehouse there. There is one thing I would like to raise here, this document shows unequivocally that we're talking about the port of Ploca, this was Croatia's territory. So there were warehouses in Croatia's territory where oil was being kept to be used by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also for the purposes of the military and the civilian population. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's perfectly right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Another thing that one can tell if one looks at this document is that this oil was then shipped to areas described by Mr. Mahmut Cehajic as free territory and to Zagreb as well?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, to Sarajevo. There was no other way but for these goods to on its way there cross territory that was HVO-controlled, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it had to cross HVO-controlled territory, but that territory was not considered unfree, quite the contrary; in fact, it was considered part of the so-called free territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Just about this last thing you said. The letter does not show that the HVO was included in this distribution. You, however, do claim that there was an agreement about this. This letter authorises two persons to sign the distribution order, Mr. Hadjit [phoen] Devic and Mr. Mahmut Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. The Mahmut Cehajic in this document is Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic's brother or at least that's what I believe. He was in charge of the logistics as well. No HVO members or, indeed, Croats are mentioned in this document. I believe, although I'm not certain, that had there been a request by the HVO pursuant to our previous agreement they would have had no choice but to distribute certain appropriate quantities of oil and other goods to us as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. I will now move on briefly to another topic that was raised in chief. Can we please have 1D 1521. This is a letter that Mate Boban and you signed on the 18th of January, 1993. My learned friend Mr. Karnavas asked you questions about some portions of the letter, but there's one thing that I would like to ascertain. Towards the bottom of page 1, I think the English and the Croatian copies are the same in this respect: "The Republic of BH defence minister, following our approval, gave an order for all of the three national armies, in keeping with the decisions of the Geneva Conference should withdraw to their own provinces, which should be an effective move in relation to the aggressor Serb army which was also supposed to withdraw." We're looking at an order issued by the defence minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can we now please go to our next document, it's the next document in that binder, this is 2D 1409. Just by way of confirmation, is this the order that you invoked a while ago, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the order, it was signed by the defence minister, Bozo Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I'd like to move on briefly, as I said, to something that I had announced, something that was not raised in chief. Mr. Akmadzic, throughout 1992 to be more specific or late in 1992 and in 1993 were you in touch with Mr. Bagaric from the health centre of the HVO defence, something to do with medical supplies, medical aid, for both the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you remember anything about that? I'm trying to slow down just to make sure that everything is reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I do remember that. We agreed that appropriate bodies in the HVO, as well as appropriate bodies in the BH army, should cooperate in this regard. We also agreed that the health ministry which was part of the government of which I was prime minister would also be working along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, excuse me, on the record I do not find what we're talking about, the number of the document. It seems that it is the next one, 2D 544, but I did not find that in the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't even refer to the document. I'm building up a foundation in order to then be able to continue to ask questions based on specific documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Speaking of documents, let us first look at this other document that you told us a little about this is 2D 705, that's the following one, that's the one after 2D 544, this was a letter that was addressed to you, a letter addressed to you by Mr. Bagaric on the 21st of December, that's what we're talking about, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It follows from this letter that Mr. Bagaric was in contact with Mr. Robert Simon, president of the International Medical Corps of California who shipped some aid to the HVO. Mr. Bagaric, however, is now adamant that the aid should go to the BH army, and that is why he wants you to write another letter that he would co-sign together with you as well as the chief medical officer of the BH army. Is that what follows from this?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this is more in reference to future aid rather than the aid that had arrived up until this point, and I think it's more about the two armies, the BH army and the HVO. It's not about the 3rd Army, the remaining army, so to speak, that's why we were required to as good as provide a definition of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were supposed to say loud and clear in a we were victims of an aggression in order to be able to receive aid like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So the previous document that we skipped is 2D 544, and it is a document in which Mr. Bagaric is addressing the commander of the medical corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the main surgeon of BH, offering the possibility of the two of them asking assistance from this non-governmental organization together. And this completes the subject matter we've just been discussing; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I took certain steps through our health ministry along those lines, I don't know whether the main surgeon in the BH -- or rather, whether the BH army had that title, but certainly something that corresponded to it, whether it was chief surgeon or something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now to round off that topic of oil, weapons, and so on, this document speaks of the existence of cooperation, does it not, between the BH army and the HVO in the struggle against a joint enemy, and that was the Serbs -- or as you said yesterday in response to a question from the Judge, evidence of the partnership in that joint struggle against the aggressor, or rather, against the Serbs during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I use the term partnership because we didn't have a Joint Command formed at that time. We had two armies that were component parts of the BH armed forces. We had the Supreme Command, which was the Presidency, and the defence minister, we had a joint defence minister, so that in fact we did not have a Joint Command. So that is why I speak about partner armies and not one and the same army. But in fact they were the same armed force, the same armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This was the topic that was touched upon during the examination-in-chief. I'd like to -- that was not touched upon during the examination-in-chief, and now I'd like to go on to another subject which was the subject of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. One follow-up question, Witness. You have just spoken about the Joint Command and about the parts played respectively by the HVO and the BH army, and I'm not quite satisfied with your answer. I want to know more. The Joint Command, as it was envisaged by the Presidency, if you go back to what can be seen usually on the ground, think of Iraq or Afghanistan when there are several armies, there is always one commander above it all because there may be a Joint Command, but as such it is necessary to have one not many commanders. Now, in the situation that you experienced, now how could that problem be solved when you had two armies and a Joint Command, wasn't there a need for one single leader? And if there was such a leader who was the civilian superior of the military leader, was it the Presidency as a whole or was it the president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was the Presidency as a whole, as an entity. The War Presidency, of which I was a member, so I myself was part of the Supreme Command. Now, in response to your question about the Joint Command in the military sense, I had said that we still had not formed a Joint Command in that sense. It was much later on that that Joint Command was formed, quite a lot later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, that is the reason why you used the word "partner," if I understood you correctly, precisely because a Joint Command did not exist?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And when the Vance-Owen Plan was evolved, you wanted to establish that kind of Joint Command so that there should not be a conflict let alone that the conflict should start?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan did provide for a Joint Command, we insisted on upon that, there was discussion about it, but as I've already said it was to be established only much later on, around the Washington Accords.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm not going to go back to that. We heard quite a lot about it during the examination-in-chief, and you explained it very well, I think, the reason for which the Joint Command was not established sooner. But this was just a continuation of the explanation of what you said earlier on. I'd like to ask you now to take a look once again briefly at document 1D 00509, and it has the force of law, a decree with the power of law, on the establishment and work of districts which the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina passed following a government recommendation.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, for my cross-examination I'd like us to look at Article 6, please, and we can see how many districts were established and under number 2 we have Bihac district, the Bihac district with headquarters in Bihac, and later on I'm going to ask you something about that particular district. But before we do that, let's take a look at another document, it is 2D 1410, the next document in line. And that document was shown to you by Mr. Karnavas as well. It is an authorisation which Mr. Alija Izetbegovic signed for Zijad Demirovic, president of the Regional Board for the SDA for Herzegovina so that he could head the expert team to be set up by the Regional Board and then undertake certain actions. What I'd like to ask you is this: Since this deals with the establishment of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, does this document show that Mr. Izetbegovic preferred to have this establishment done through the SDA, that is to say the political party which he led, was that your experience, rather than through the official organs of the elected powers and authorities elected at the first democratic elections?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that when we're talking about the Muslims the SDA party was victorious so that in that area it was his wish and right to use that channel, to say that the representatives of the Muslim people should hold negotiations with the representatives of Croatian people. And he decided to take that step, and I don't think it was a very auspicious one, not a good one. But he decided to work through the SDA and that was a parallel form of work, actually, within the Presidency that I've already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Does this document in fact confirm that during the agreements and negotiation -- or rather, during developing the agreement, does this confirm that it just actually represents the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it just represents the Muslim people, and this authorisation we see has just his signature, no stamp, no Presidency mentioned anywhere, and at the top it says "democratic action," not Presidency of the BH. So this authorisation refers to him solely as president of the party and not president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you to tell us something about this -- well, a little while ago one of the Judges asked a witness a question here, I can't mention his name, but were there other Presidency members who worked outside Sarajevo during the war, especially members of the Presidency of the Muslim ethnicity? And I'm -- I'm saying Muslim, but I know that after the Dayton Accords that ethnicity was referred to as the Bosniaks. But as we are discussing 1992, that period of time, without insulting anyone I'm using the same terms that you're using. Am I right there?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So taking this period of 1992, from the beginning of the war, let's say April onwards, were there members of the Presidency who for a time acted outside the Presidency, or rather, who left Sarajevo in other words?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Presidency passed a decision moreover to the following effect, that some members of the Presidency may leave Sarajevo, although they could not be prohibited from leaving Sarajevo but they could be allowed to do so, in order to organize political activities and a system of defence where they would be going. And in this specific case, in response to your question, from Sarajevo Mr. Franjo Boris left and Mr. Fikret Abdic left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you, as my question referred to the Muslim Presidency members, that we focus precisely on Fikret Abdic. Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly who the man was, what the results were at the first democratic elections, how Mr. Abdic did there, when he left Sarajevo, and whether he disagreed with Alija Izetbegovic's policy in that year of 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and be brief, otherwise it could be a very long and involved story. During the Yugoslav period, the communist period, Mr. Fikret Abdic was the director of Agrokomerc a large firm in western Bosnia. At the elections or the pre-electoral campaign in actual fact, the SDA party led the campaign but did not have much success until Fikret Abdic joined the party. Once Fikret Abdic had joined the party, especially at the rallies that were held, people came to them, double the amount of people came to these rallies, he was very popular in Bosnia and Herzegovina especially in the Bihac and Cazin and Kladusa areas. At the elections for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina on behalf of the SDA party Fikret Abdic won, Izetbegovic and Ganic -- Izetbegovic as a Muslim and Ganic as the others, and the most votes were secured by Fikret Abdic. And he and many others - I'm not going to say all of them - but many others expected him to become president of the Presidency. Mr. Izetbegovic, as president of the SDA party, won the support in the Main Board of the party, where the decisions are made, that he should be nominated as president of the Presidency, and that was what was done, he was. However, Fikret Abdic was bitter about this as far as I know, but he didn't express his bitterness at the Presidency meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me now whether you know when he left Sarajevo, that's the second part of my question, and whether while he was a member of the Presidency he expressed his disagreement with the positions taken by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic; and if so, what points did they disagree on?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fikret Abdic did leave Sarajevo as far as I remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Judge Trechsel has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Without wishing to teach you lessons or interfere, I think you have now several times asked four or five different questions in one, and I was suggesting that one might even gain time if you put them one by one, let him answer; next one. Because as we have seen it is so much that towards the end you have to ask the question again. Just as an attempt at assisting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. I wanted to move forward faster, but obviously I'm not doing that, so I'll take it one by one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me go back to my question. When according to you did Fikret Abdic leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was around July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And where did he go?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went to Kladusa, where is western Bosnia, whole area of western Bosnia. His firm -- not his firm, a state firm Agrokomerc was in Kladusa and through his activities as a politician he covered the whole of western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you remember, which issues did Fikret Abdic -- or rather, what subjects did Mr. Fikret Abdic disagree with Izetbegovic, on what issues?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few issues. I'd like to stress here that Mr. Fikret Abdic was not satisfied with the way in which the meetings were prepared. He was dissatisfied with the topics discussed at the meetings because he insisted that the Presidency should discuss economic topics, give priority to economics. He was dissatisfied with the discussions over Bosnia's internal set-up, and he was even dissatisfied with the organization of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did he express his dissatisfaction with the Islamization of the Bosnian army at the time or immediately afterwards in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the material time, the time we're discussing now, he didn't expressly bring that up; however, he did speak about that subject later on and he sent documents to the Presidency, he sent them through me too, because when I was the general secretary that's what I would do, I would convey these documents. And when he became conscious of the fact or when it became obvious that the army was moving towards Islamization, he stood up against it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at another document, it's 2D, and it's the last document I'm going to put to you, 2D 1408 is the number, and it's a document which was signed precisely by Mr. Fikret Abdic, it is information about some characteristics in the Bihac district -- about the situation in the Bihac district, the date is the 14th of April, 1993. I think you've seen this document before, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then we'll just say that he describes the existing situation on page 1 and 2, then he goes on to -- well, this document is linked to the establishment of the districts and the decree that had the force of law, districts and their work and functioning, and he sets all this out in this piece of information. He says that everything is going badly and that the political cadres are paying more attention to themselves than to state interests, but what is important for us here is to be found on page 4. That's the Croatian reference. It's page 3 in the English, the last paragraph on that page. Fikret Abdic talks about some problems that were widespread throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, but these problems are of particular importance to us here. It says: "This idea, this danger that was on account of great conspicuity notice, created, designed elaborated on, well-argued, and most importantly implemented by preserving the rest of commodity reserves foreign currency saved up by the population and by saving up more than 50 million mark that the population would have to pay for because of rising prices which would follow as a result. A theory was tabled in opposition to this that this temporary deduction of foreign means of payment was aimed against the Republic of the BH, its sovereignty, meaning against the people. This would have constituted a case of serious manipulation involving the people of the BH, because neither the BH dinar could have been accepted because of the interruption of cash flow, undue interventions, unrealistic foreign currency rate, unequal distribution of funds throughout municipalities, communication blockades with the remaining parts of the Republic of B&H and because of not being able to obtain raw material and auxiliary goods to ensure means of payment outside the Bihac district." Mr. Akmadzic, what seems to follow from this is that Mr. Abdic on a temporary basis introduced the German mark as a means of payment, as a currency, precisely because of the problems he's here referring to, and because of that he was accused of undermining the sovereignty and the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as everything else. He's here explaining a number of technical problems that he was facing with the currency in the Bihac area. Do you remember the situation being the way he describes it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you refer to these as technical problems. They weren't just technical problems, they were problems that went deeper than that. I mean, it wasn't just the Bihac area, it was further afield as well. This goes back to the very beginning of the war. The Yugoslav dinar, which then still existed as a valid currency in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was a worthless piece of paper, that's how he described it. You could only use this currency in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You could purchase the goods and then sell them at a higher price and in exchange for a proper currency elsewhere, outside Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Bosnia and Herzegovina it was very difficult to introduce money. Money, currency, was produced abroad and then because of the blockade around Sarajevo it was very difficult to get it into Bosnia, it was very difficult to start using it, and this new currency was not something that came from the national bank, it was more like vouchers rather than money.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise. To be quite specific, you're talking about the BH dinar, that's what Mr. Abdic is talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at first it was the Yugoslav dinar and then we had the BH dinar. It was very difficult to get it into circulation because of all these problems Croatia's dinar or the German mark were still being used in some parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a legitimate currency of payment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's move on to other problems faced by the Bihac district, if you look at page 6 in the Croatian, and I think in the English the reference is page 5, paragraph 2, what is it saying, what is Mr. Abdic saying there in April of 1994? He says in April 1993 the regulations passed by the highest authorities reached this area a half a year later than they were supposed to. When they eventually reached the area, one could tell that the provisions envisaged in those regulations were impossible to implement because they did not apply to the state of war. They were particularly impossible to carry through in an area that was entirely encircled. There was no communication at all and no directives from the republican bodies. You are aware of the problems addressed here by Mr. Abdic. In purely geographical terms I think everyone here knows about the distance between Bihac and Sarajevo, and that's precisely what he's talking about, this impossibility to communicate?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm perfectly aware of those problems. I'm aware of the problems faced by Bihac while I was under siege. I'm aware of the problems that kept occurring as the war went on. I know about the fact that the cooperation between the HVO and the BH army in that area was particularly good, despite the fact that our chief HVO commander in the area had been killed. They were working well together, but this did not shield them from accusations. The accusations came in a way from Sarajevo, and these accusations even went as far as to insinuate that what they wanted was to join Croatia, which was simply untrue. I think this is another subject that Mr. Fikret Abdic addressing in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just two brief explanations just to make sure we're on the same page. What is the distance between -- there is one thing that I wanted to ask you, something else. The period in time that we're considering, what was the ethnic breakdown of the Bihac area and its population?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say off the top of my head. We have the 1991 census. The entire Bihac area was predominantly populated by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will not be showing you other portions of this text talking about problems faced by other regions, not just the Bihac region, therefore I'm just trying to walk you through this to confirm a number of things for me. We have another such document here to do with a member of the Presidency who is a Muslim. The next paragraph is very interesting: Fines, compensation for damages, interest rates and expenses for court proceedings can be determined only on Yugoslav dinars. That's what you've been talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Prison sentences of more than six months cannot be carried out as the district has no prison facilities that could hold such convicts. Moreover, the degrees entailed in these proceedings remain the same as before the war. The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Supreme Court is still the state body in third instance, and there is no contact with it and there has not been since April 1992. These are matters to do with the judiciary, and this is precisely what we've often found ourselves caught up in discussing here in this courtroom. Abdic says, if I understand this correctly, as follows: Confirm that for my benefit, please, that the fines incurred were still being expressed in Yugoslav dinars and there was no communication with the Supreme Court, not even in April 1993; therefore, it was impossible for the judicial system to operate properly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what Mr. Fikret is saying here, he's talking about a number of problems, he's talking about this problem of separation, in terms of geography and in terms of distance. Bihac is about a five-hour drive away if you don't make stopovers. Sarajevo is encircled. The state did not pass all the appropriate regulations about the financial situation, currency, money, how this money was to be used in practical terms, traffic fines, that sort of thing. The BH Presidency closed down two principal prisons in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Foca and Zenica. Mr. Fikret warns that convicts had nowhere to be sent to. This is a problem occurring throughout his area, Bihac, Cazin, Kladusa, and other neighbouring areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: These are problems, as long as I'm correct, to do with this because the central authorities back in 1993 did not react in good time and did not pass appropriate regulations in good time to deal in particular with this situation, the situation having to do with these areas that were encircled and under siege by the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Bihac had been under siege for quite a long time. At the very end of war, in 1995, it was finally liberated. This is when I eventually travelled to Bihac. I visited the area, and I saw for myself how good the cooperation was between the HVO and the BH army. I brought in humanitarian aid in several lorries. It was Mr. Prlic, of all people, who had asked me to please go to that area because I was in Zagreb at the time, therefore Bihac wasn't as far away as it would have been for him. The cooperation was very good. The people in the HVO refused to receive aid that would not have been given to the BH army as well because they wanted everyone to have an equal share.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, we just discussed the example of Bihac. Nevertheless, these problems were occurring throughout Herzegovina, throughout the Tuzla area as well, throughout the Zenica area because the regulations passed by the central authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina applied throughout the republic, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but even districts that were set up then were in fact functioning properly. Therefore, there was a lot of discord, a lot of disagreement as to how regulations were to be applied throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, Mr. Fikret Abdic eventually, and this is something that we can find at page 7 of this document, this is page 6 in the English, paragraph 2, paragraph 3 as well, he goes on to sum up the situation as follows: He says the situation has been remedied, legitimate delegates were appointed throughout the district. I think this is a fair summary. Do you know that back in 1993 Fikret Abdic, precisely because of all these problems with the Sarajevo government - and we've been talking about a lot about that, the government, I mean the Presidency, I mean the disagreements with the army, I mean the disagreements with Mr. Izetbegovic - is this not why Mr. Abdic eventually proclaimed the existence of an autonomous western Bosnia area in that region?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fikret Abdic never agreed with the way the state was run or the way the talks were unfolding at Presidency meetings. Mr. Abdic was always in favour of talks. He wanted peace to be achieved through talks. He was fully in favour of the Vance-Owen Plan. He accepted all of the other plans as well. I did spend a great deal of time talking to him, and in Geneva we talked a lot too. Sometimes he would go to the talks in Geneva and sometimes not simply because it was very difficult to leave the Bihac area. UNPROFOR once flew in a helicopter to get him out of the area and take him to Geneva. Eventually he chose the solution which he believed was the best one. He set up a provisional government in the Bihac area and eventually it got off the ground and started operating quite well. In fact, there is another thing that I wish to say now, now that I'm talking about this, Mr. Fikret arranged for money to be sent from international aid, to be sent to each and every individual that it was addressed to. For example, you have someone in Germany and they send money to their brother who is still in Bihac, for example, 500 German mark, 1.000 German mark. The important thing was to make sure the money would reach its addressee, and he organized ways for this to happen. Fikret Abdic was a much loved man in his area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Akmadzic, did armed clashes erupt between Fikret Abdic's men and the BH army late in 1993 precisely because of these clashing notions that they entertained and how the Republic of B&H should be run?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were armed clashes that eventually erupted. I didn't go to the area and see it myself, therefore I can't say anything about that, despite which Mr. Fikret Abdic was precisely convinced that the Islamic circles headed by Izetbegovic and the people around him trying to frame him and even tried to kill him. He once even went so far as to tell me, I won't let them kill me. He told me this in Geneva. The armed clashes were high-intensity ones and this is one of the typical features of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and this is something I haven't been mentioning so far. I told you about definition provided by the Presidency at the very outset. Nevertheless, in Bosnia and Herzegovina it is obvious that there are some elements of civil war at work although the war has a whole could not be viewed as a civil war, specifically I mean what happened in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend Ms. Senka, I'm sorry, but I think there is an enormous error in the transcript, page 24, line 9, there is a check there which means that the transcript will be completed, but I think for the benefit of everyone's understanding, the Chamber's understanding, it should be said that the witness talked about Islamic circles surrounding Alija Izetbegovic and Alija Izetbegovic himself. I apologise for this interruption to my learned friend, Ms. Senka.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much to my learned friend Ms. Vesna Alaburic. I was listening to the witness and I was not following the transcript. Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Finally my last question. We spoke about these clashes, this conflict among the Muslims, can you confirm for us - and this is something -- this is a question I have raised several times but let me be as specific as I possibly can - did this conflict arise because of the clashing notions among the Muslims on how Bosnia should be set up, specifically clashes between Fikret Abdic on the one hand and Alija Izetbegovic and the circles around him on the other?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness, this completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours, this completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I just have a follow-up question for you. Ms. Nozica mostly spoke about Bihac and Fikret Abdic. I listened to her questions and her -- and your answers, and thought about Herzegovina. Here's my question: You were the prime minister of the government. In every state the government acts via administrations, through decrees and laws, ensures that public order is respected, makes sure that justice functions well, those are the main characteristics of a state. The siege of Sarajevo started probably on the 5th of April, 1992, or let's say during that month of April. And when there's a siege Sarajevo was encircled by Serbian forces and one might wonder how the state functioned and what was the link between the government, the municipalities, the districts, the regions, and so on and so forth. You were right in the middle of things. Were you under the impression that the state continued to function or do you believe that there was Sarajevo, Mr. Izetbegovic, the Presidency, a few administrations, but do you think that the municipalities on the outside had to work on their own because they could not rely upon the help from Sarajevo because I remember the last document which we saw on Bihac. In a nutshell, could you tell me whether you as prime minister believed that your decisions were implemented on the field or were you helpless because every village, every municipality, had to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely, Your Honour, that's it. And I'd like to add, although we don't have much time, that the Presidency could not extend its power and authority all over the state for the reasons that you have stated. And secondly, I would like to say that we, the Croat members of the Presidency, asked that it be relocated so that it could function. Had the Presidency gone out of Sarajevo, as were the strategic military plans, that in case of war the capital should be left behind and the Presidency moved to where the supreme authority could function, I mentioned Livno because there were the necessary prerequisites for that, that's the first point. And the second point is that Fikret Abdic for those reasons and also for political reasons with respect to the political set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina found it and proclaimed in a way the province of western Bosnia, is what he called it, because the Vance-Owen Plan envisaged a western Bosnian province. The names -- took the names of the towns, and so this was the Bihac province. And Fikret Abdic insisted that the Vance-Owen Plan plan be put into effect as well as other plans that came about later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, sir. I'm now turning to the 5D and 6D, but I understood that they gave their time away. Is that so? 5D?

utterances.speaker: MR. PLAVEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no questions for this witness and we ceded our time to the Stojic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So that part of the cross-examination is over. I suggest we have now a 20-minute break so that Mr. Scott can get prepared for his cross-examination. We shall then resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing's resumed. Mr. Scott, the Trial Chamber wants to know clearly what you plan. Do you want to use all the six hours, all of them, or less than six hours or don't you know right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First off, good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everyone and counsel, everyone in and around the courtroom. I would have to guess, Mr. President, that I will use the six hours, but of course if we make more progress than that, then so much the better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I'd like to start off, sir, asking a couple questions about Mr. Izetbegovic, who has featured rather prominently in the questioning over the past few days. It might assist you if I tell you this, it is of course not my function here to defend anyone, except perhaps the victims of the alleged crimes in the case. I'm not here to defend Mr. Izetbegovic, and I will also tell you that, as the Chamber has heard, everyone knows this was a horrible, terrible war in which there were victims on all sides. There were many Croat victims, and of course I'm sure you know that this institution prosecutes and tries accused from all ethnic groups, Serb, Croat, and Muslim. In that respect, however, just so the record is clear in connection with Mr. Izetbegovic and your dealings with him, I would like to remind you and ask you some questions about what you said in your testimony in the Kordic case, and I'm referring to page 2 -- excuse me, 20319 on the 5th of June, 2000, a little more than eight years ago, I'm afraid. And you said: "I'm very good friends with Mr. Izetbegovic. While I was secretary-general we visited Rome together and we called on the Pope, although he's a Muslim and I'm a Catholic. He's a Muslim of Islamic faith and I'm a Croat of Catholic faith. Together we visited Tehran. We knew each other well. I even called on him at home where he lived. He's a good man. He's an honest politician; however, there are interests that transcend individual interest." Now, if you're able to follow along on that, sir, and if you need me to I'll read it to you again. Do you stand by that assessment, description, of your relationship and dealings with Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by them. But I can say that perhaps I overemphasized the fact that we were very good friends, perhaps I went too far. We were on very good terms. Perhaps that would be a better way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have in front of me what you said in the French version. There may be somebody to be added here: "I am quite a good friend of Mr. Izetbegovic's whilst I was secretary-general we went -- we were in Rome to visit the Pope. I am a Catholic and he's a Muslim." And then you continue: "I am of Islamic faith [as interpreted], and he is a Catholic Christian [as interpreted], that is what is in the transcript." Was that something you added or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said, we went to visit the Pope together. We visited Tehran together, but when we -- he received a private audience, a separate audience with the Pope, it's a private audience as it's called with the Pope. And in Tehran he went without me to see their religious leader, I think it was Hamnaj [phoen], and we went to see foreign minister Vela Jacic [phoen] together, as we did to the president of the republic, Raf-sandjani; we went there to see President Raf-sandjani, and we also visited the mosques together, but I don't think that is relevant for this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'm at a bit of a loss, Your Honour, because of the way something was transcribed. On page 29, line 17, what was read to the witness was, I am of Islamic faith and he is a Catholic Christian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what I have in the Kordic case, and perhaps there was a difference between the English and the French version is that he, Mr. Izetbegovic, is an Islam of Muslim faith, and I, referring to yourself, I am a Catholic, is that correct, a Croat of Catholic faith?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a Croat Catholic. Mr. Izetbegovic is of the Islamic religious faith, and he was very respected in the Islamic world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in connection with your references to he's -- he was a good man -- or of course at that time he was still alive. He's a good man. He's an honest politician, accepting for the moment that of course you may have had strong political disagreements with him, again do you stand by your assessment that he was fundamentally an honest and good man?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His attitude to me and in his attitude as I was able to see to others, he was an honest man, but he was bad in politics and that's what proved to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, he may or may not have been a good politician, we can agree with that. You described him in the Kordic testimony, of course, and as you confirmed a few moments ago as an honest politician. With that in mind, let's turn to this topic once again of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when did you first become the general secretary of that body, because as I understand it you had already took that position or held that position prior to the time following the elections in November 1990 that Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Boras, and others took their positions. So when did you first become the general secretary of the -- of that body?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what you wish to hear. When Mr. Izetbegovic came to the Presidency and the other members of the Presidency as well, of course, I was an advisor in the presidential offices of the president; and in his cabinet or offices before Izetbegovic the president was Obrad Piljak from amongst the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And approximately when, sir, my question, my real question, was simply to put some more time on some of these points, when had you first taken up that position which maybe was described differently at the time, but was or came to be known as general secretary of the Presidency, of that body?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The posts were named the same. We didn't change anything with the arrival of the new Presidency. An advisor was one position. I was the advisor for press and information, whereas the general secretary of the Presidency was a position for the entire Presidency, and the general secretary led the entire Presidency apart from the political side of course and I was appointed general secretary - I can't give you the exact date - but I think that it was at the beginning of February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when did you -- when had you first come into the other position that you just described, as an advisor of some sort at the presidential level, if I can describe it that way? When did you take on that responsibility or function?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took over that function on the 1st of June, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at some point during that time were you ever an advisor to Mr. Izetbegovic in his individual capacity, and by that I don't mean privately. But apart from serving the Presidency as a collective body, did you ever consider yourself to be any sort of advisor or staff person to Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as a result of the 18 November 1990 elections, there was a seven-member Presidency and just so we can quickly run through them again, the two Croat representatives on the Presidency were Mr. Boras and Stjepan Kljuic; the Serb representatives or members were Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic; the two Muslims were Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Abdic that you spoke about a few minutes ago; and the other, the category that the legislation provided for as other was Mr. Ganic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that body, that -- as so composed, the Presidency functioned in that way or, again, as so composed until approximately March or April of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so we can begin to hopefully clarify and confirm at least bits of what we can and see what disputes may or may not be left. So there's no question that up until that point in time, March 1992, the Presidency was legal and legitimate in the way that we've been discussing it this week; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then as a result of the increasing and then open conflict with the Serbs, in early April 1992 the two Serb members, Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic withdrew from the Presidency, and around that time, on about the 8th of April, 1991 -- excuse me, 1992, something called -- some people refer to as the War Presidency or perhaps an expanded Presidency was established; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we talk about the expansion of the Presidency, let's also go back and take it step by step in terms of this office called the president of the Presidency. So in December -- in approximately December 1990 Mr. Izetbegovic was elected by the other members of the Presidency as president of the Presidency, and again I assume from everything I've heard in the last week or so that there's no dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No dispute about that in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as I understood something you said, I believe it was yesterday if I recall, one of the last couple of days, is that the function of the -- the selection or naming of the president was not done as a result of a popular vote, it didn't come from the electorate as a whole and it was not something governed by the constitution, but it was governed by the rules of procedure of the Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We called it the rules of procedure of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And how were those rules established, by the way? Who adopted those rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the previous rules of procedure that had existed for the previous Presidency and on the basis of the constitution that we were all well aware of, the professional services tabled a proposal for the rules of procedure for the Presidency, and then at its first meeting the Presidency adopted the rules of procedure for the Presidency, and I've already spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, do we need to take any sort of -- we have a mechanic problem here behind the Bench. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may proceed, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That was off the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'd all like to have a still photo of that from the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Akmadzic. All right. So we're talking about the rules of procedure, and if the rules of procedure were to be adopted or amended from time to time, I take it they would come before the Presidency and the Presidency would vote on whether to adopt new or amended rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And pursuant to those procedures then, around the 20th of December, 1991, after Mr. Izetbegovic had completed his first term, he was elected by a vote of the Presidency to a second term, which then would have run approximately from about the 20th of December, 1991, to 20 December 1992, and that vote and that process was also legal and legitimate; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, and I've already described that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Although I do understand that by that time, perhaps because of the growing conflict or tension, the Serb members of the Presidency as of December 1991, Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic, voted against Mr. Izetbegovic, so it was not a unanimous vote but a majority decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Mr. Fikret Abdic voted against, so there were three votes against.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So if there were seven -- if my very basic math -- arithmetic is correct, there were four votes for, assuming if Mr. Izetbegovic himself voted, and three votes against. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or, rather, yes, yes, that's right, four were in favour yes. Four votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving forward from that we talked already about Ms. Plavsic and Koljevic resigning, their resignations were accepted or acknowledged in the minutes of the meeting on the 9th of April, 1993. And you may recall, I don't know that we need to look at the minutes again, but the Chamber has again recently, with another witness whose name I will not mention, look at the minutes of a meeting held in early April 1993, including on the 8th or 9th, if the courtroom thinks at some point that we should look at those, of course we can. But you were in attendance at those meetings. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind specifically, but I did attend the meeting, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, I have nothing really specific in mind, except that according to the minutes of those meetings, which the Chamber has seen before, one set of minutes for the 4th, 5th, 6th, and 8th of April being P 10484, in which you were listed as being present and Exhibit P 10485, which is the -- are the minutes for the 9th of April in which you were also present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, in the service of equality of arms, would you be so kind as to indicate the number of the binder we have to open?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It should be in binder number 3, I believe. And I said, I was really not intending to get into those, but just to tell me the witness what I'm referring to. But if it helps, if it helps, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you will look at first of all then at 10484. As I said a moment ago, these are the minutes for sessions on the 4th, 5th, 6th, and 8th of April, 1992, and if you'll look on the first page roughly around the middle of the page -- I'm sorry, you're still -- 10484. Perhaps the usher can assist.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You'll see that you are listed above the -- a little above the middle of the page as being present. Do you see that, sir? I'm sorry, apparently not. Do you see the record, sir, indicating your presence at those meetings as reflected in the minutes?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that the meeting of the 9th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at P 10484, these are the minutes for the 4th, 5th, 6th, and 8th of April, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you look at the very -- what I hope would be the next exhibit, 10485, I believe that you will see that that is the record -- those are the minutes of the meeting on the 9th of April, 1992, and if the record is correct indicates that you also attended that meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Now, at those meetings you will recall I believe on the 8th of April, 1992, an expanded Presidency given the imminent threat or existence of a condition of war that was declared on that day, which is reflected in the minutes and also in a decree. On that day an expanded Presidency was established which, is it correct - this is my question to you - in addition to the seven persons that we've identified so far by position, I'm saying by position not by the names of the person holding those positions, but included the president of the government or prime minister, the president of the National Assembly or some might say parliament, and the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff or essentially the senior military professional, the senior commander of the armed forces of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, those three additional persons were added to the seven members to make up the expanded Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again - and I'm just going to again take this step by step - that was all legal and legitimate; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we look at -- what I've done hopefully to save some time and to be as clear as possible if I can find it, if you can turn to -- sorry - that has been marked as P 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, because you're moving onto another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to remain with this document for a few seconds, which is the minutes of the meetings on the 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th of April, the latter date being important because that's the day when the imminent threat of war was proclaimed. Witness, I was about to say Mr. Secretary-General at the time because you were there, you're here to authenticate the minutes, I discover that, in fact, there was a recording, an audio recording of the discussions that took place over the four days. That's the last sentence in the text. In fact, what we have here is a synopsis, a summary, of the decisions that were taken. Looking at the B/C/S document, because here we were working on the -- with the English text, but I looked at the B/C/S version, and curiously enough I failed to see your signature, it is missing. Well, normally speaking we all in this courtroom in our previous lives have had to draft minutes of meetings, among other things. So normally when there's a meeting there's at least one person, if not two, signing the minutes of the meeting. So normally you should have signed it, you should have signed the minutes of the decisions that were made; but we fail to see your signature in the B/C/S text. Can you tell me why? Because the document should have been signed by the secretary-general and by the president of the Presidency, but we see no signature at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the departure of two Serbian members of the Presidency, a number of Serb workers or people who worked in the Presidency left too, so it was difficult to organize the work, all the technical work, that had to be done, recordings, typing, adoption of the minutes, things like that. The minutes were usually signed after adoption at the next Presidency meeting, and obviously in that time of war, because there wasn't enough electricity and because the conditions under which the Presidency worked in general were made more difficult, matters like that were difficult. And that's why these particular minutes were not signed on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard your answer, but this is the 65th Session which was held on the 4th, 5th, 6th, and 8th of April, and then we have the 66th Session, which was held on the 9th of April at noon. You were there as well. Looking at the agenda I see that no mention is made of that previous -- those previous minutes, no approval is mentioned, but I might be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the reason for this. I don't think the minutes were produced at the time, and that's why it couldn't be tendered for adoption. This is something that was bound to happen again because we had reached an agreement at a Presidency meeting that if no minutes could be taken, we should at least try to tape-record the proceedings as frequently as possible. Should those prove impossible to transcribe, they should just be filed away. As soon as the right conditions were in place, we said all the minutes and all the transcripts would eventually get written up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back for a moment. I was going to direct you to another exhibit but we'll come to that momentarily. But in connection with the expanded Presidency which we were talking about a moment or two ago, is it also correct, sir, that the constitution also provided that one of the characteristics or functions or features, if you will, of this expanded Presidency was that it had expanded powers? For example, it could carry out what might be described as both executive and legislative powers or functions.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And it may be worth just momentarily pausing on Exhibit P 00150, and that should be in the first binder. This is a compilation of three decrees, the first one -- one on the first page, I think you will see this is the decree by which the name of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina was changed, deleting the word "socialist" from the name of the state. The second is a decree or regulation on abolishing or doing away with the Territorial Defence organization that had existed until the former Yugoslavia as part of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to replace that with the new Territorial Defence being the proclaimed armed forces of the state of the -- the new state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then if you'll see on the third decision being the proclamation of an immediate threat of war which in Article 2 again indicates the membership of the Presidency being expanded to include the positions that I had mentioned to you a few minutes ago. All of that is correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't actually see this, but I know that what you're suggesting is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm sorry if you can't, but thank you for that. I don't think there will be any question about that; if there is, I'm sure I'll be corrected. Now, if I could ask you to go to P 10495, and that will be in the third binder, it should be the -- yes. It may be helpful to have that -- yes, you have that both in English and there is a Croatian version for the witness and for others. So that we can be as specific as possible and hopefully move as efficiently as possible, I put this information in front of you. Now, based on your testimony so far, I think we can agree, I hope, that as to the time-period on the first -- the first time-period, December 1990 to the 8th of April, 1992, that information appears to be consistent with your evidence this afternoon and there's no dispute about that. Now, if we can then focus on the time-period from the 9th of April to approximately - I say approximately - the 20th of December, 1992, under the expanded or so-called War Presidency. This would indicate that in addition to the seven members above, and of course Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic have left by this time, Mr. Hasan Efendic was named -- not named but became a member of the expanded Presidency by function of his position as head of the armed forces; Mr. Jure Pelivan, who had I think by this time assumed the role of prime minister in the place of one of the Serbs who had left because I believe Mr. Krajisnik, Momcilo Krajisnik, had ceased being the speaker or president of the Assembly and Mr. Pelivan had taken his place -- excuse me, my mistake. Strike that --

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think you made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I did, you're absolutely right. Mr. Pelivan was prime minister, then it was Mr. Krajisnik who had left as president of the parliament or Assembly, and he had been replaced by the Croat, Mr. Ljubic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the vice-president of the Assembly or the vice chairman of the Assembly at the time that Mr. Krajisnik was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So it was logical when Mr. Krajisnik left, Mr. Ljubic as the deputy took that position. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So at that point in time -- and I've listed you here because you were certainly an important feature, I won't say member, but an important participant in those meetings. So I've just put your name here so we don't forget about you, as I'm sure we wouldn't. But everyone above that point at that moment as approximately the 9th of April, that was the existing expanded Presidency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, aside from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then I just note and so that there's no confusion about the diagram or chart, whatever one wants to call it, I've indicated that Mr. Sefer Halilovic actually replaced Mr. Efendic quite quickly, just a few weeks later, and so -- but again filled the position of head of the armed forces. And that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then below your name, some weeks later I believe, is it correct, do you recall that it was in approximately early June of 1992 that new Serb members were named to the Presidency to replace Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic, and there was Mirko Pejanovic and Nenad Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And again, my understanding - and correct me if I'm wrong, please - they were named on the basis that in terms of the election in November of 1990 they had been the Serb members, the members of the representatives of the Serb political party, who had received the next-most votes and therefore were in line, if you will, to fill these positions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is debatable, because they belonged to parties that had lost the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Do you know how it was that those two particular Serbs became elected or placed on the Presidency at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle was the one that you explained in terms of the votes garnered, they came second, but it was because of the parties and that's why I called it debatable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Very well. And then just to -- they're not members of the -- well, one was, Mr. Efendic and then subsequently Mr. Halilovic, but again just to have these positions on the paper, so to speak, the three senior military commanders at this time - and this is also reflected in the minutes of the meetings that we looked at a few minutes ago, if we need to look at them again - you had Mr. Efendic, quickly followed by Mr. Halilovic as the head of the armed forces, Mr. Siber, a Croat as the number two, if you will, and Mr. Jovan Divjak, a Serb as the operations officer. And those three persons representing the three senior officers of the -- Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you a similar question that I asked you about the top of the page. As its described here, did that Presidency continue to function from approximately the 9th of April, then, of 1992 until the end of that year, approximately on the 20th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what were those other changes, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic left the Presidency, roughly speaking, because of the same reasons as Mr. Koljevic and Ms. Plavsic. I don't think he formally resigned. He just took off and he went to Belgrade -- or at least that's as much as we could learn at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. And apart from then the departure of Mr. Kecmanovic, at least physically, any other changes to the composition of that group during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were any or at least none that I can spot right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then can we agree then, sir, that the -- with an asterisk, if you will, by Mr. Kecmanovic's name, that that Presidency, that expanded Presidency, as represented here, that continued to be again a legal and legitimate Presidency until the end of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've pointed out for the benefit of the Chamber a couple of times, I'm not a lawyer. The constitution does not provide for Presidency members leaving. They may resign. The constitution provides nothing for how new members of the Presidency should be elected in this way. Therefore, I cannot really claim that this Presidency is a legal and legitimate one nor, indeed, can I deny that. It operated this way. If you want my opinion, I don't think it was entirely legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why not? And let me just jump in here, sir, and say for the past several days you've been quite free, and I'm not questioning you in having done so, to express your views as a senior government officials, as someone who was ultimately the prime minister of this country. So putting aside any technical legalese we might call it, please assist the Judges as much as you can with your personal knowledge of the workings and the status of these arrangements. Now, having said that, you've just said that this is an accurate, factual, description I believe if I can put it that way of the state of affairs, but you said a moment ago there might be some question in your mind. Can you please tell the Judges very specifically any question that occurs to you about the legitimacy of this Presidency as so composed.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
